title: Banks, Crypto and PayPal Make Their Case at Singapore FinTech Festival
snippet: A $6.3 billion crypto heist, PayPal’s reinvention and AI moving our money. Georgia Hanias reports on a lively day at Singapore FinTech Festival. The post Banks, Crypto and PayPal Make Their Case at Singapore FinTech Festival appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Binance, Ripple, J.P. Morgan, Schroders and Banking Circle all on the same stage to debate the future of money. No wonder the room was packed.

Pitting some of the biggest names in crypto against the top dogs of traditional banking made for one of the more honest discussions on day two of Singapore FinTech Festival. There was real enthusiasm for digital assets, 24/7 markets and new ways of moving money, but also some serious warnings about the risks of automation and whether stablecoins really are the answer to the world’s payment problems.

One world, many ways to move money

Binance Co-CEO Richard Teng thinks digital assets have barely scratched the surface. With automation and round-the-clock access to financial markets creating new opportunities, he reckons there’s still around 90% of the market left to capture.

But Umar Farooq, global co-head of payments at J.P. Morgan, was more cautious about the risks of moving towards fully automated financial markets.

“As markets become fully automated, tokenised, and operate 24/7, a major disruption – even without malicious actors – could lead to severe negative outcomes,” he warned.

The discussion, which also featured Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse, Schroders CFO Meagen Burnett and Banking Circle chairman Ralph Hamers, showed just how differently the industry is thinking about the future of money.

And Binance has had a rather costly reminder of how quickly things can go wrong.

Binance’s $6.3billion test

Binance knows all about disruption, having suffered one of the biggest crypto thefts in history. Following the $6.3billion hack in October, the exchange committed to covering customer losses using its own funds, while working with industry partners to freeze around $3billion of the stolen assets.

But look what it’s doing next. Binance is planning to expand into five more Asian markets next year, without needing to raise external funds.

Teng was keen to highlight how quickly the wider crypto industry responded to the attack.

“The rails are very secure – our stablecoin partners immediately froze accounts in record speed,” he told the audience.

He believes the next priority for payments will be closer collaboration between providers, better protection against cyberattacks and services that reflect the needs of customers in different markets. For Teng, much of this comes down to building the best customer interface and understanding what people need locally.

But how quickly will digital assets become part of everyday finance?

Hamers offered a useful reality check.

“If you look at stablecoins and the volume of traffic there, it has doubled in two years, but it still represents just 0.02 per cent of all money moving in the world, so it has some time to go.”

He also sees opportunities for tokenisation to change how assets are exchanged. He suggested a future where tokenised assets could be traded directly for one another, creating something closer to a barter system without the need for money to sit between every transaction.

Teng, meanwhile, pointed to increased trading in tokenised US stocks outside American market hours as an example of how digital assets could open up investment opportunities across the world.

But Farooq questioned why stablecoins remain so heavily concentrated in US dollars.

“If stablecoins were the best thing since sliced bread, you would see stablecoins in every currency, but you don’t. Pretty much you see one currency, the US dollar.”

For all the talk about new payment rails, there’s clearly still some disagreement about what the future of money should look like.

Can PayPal become more than a checkout button?

PayPal CEO Enrique Lores also has some big plans for the future of payments, as he explained during a conversation with GFTN‘s Pat Patel.

I have to admit, it’s been a long time since I last clicked on a PayPal checkout button. I was probably still using my Hotmail account!

But Lores wants PayPal to become a much bigger part of people’s financial lives.

He challenged the assumption that PayPal could continue to grow purely through technology. As a two-sided network connecting merchants and consumers, its real strength comes from understanding and engaging with customers on both sides.

According to Lores, consumer financial services are already PayPal’s fastest-growing business, with opportunities in credit, lending and buy now, pay later (BNPL).

PayPal also has something valuable when it comes to lending: information about what consumers earn and spend. For gig-economy workers, for example, that could help the company assess borrowing needs and provide financial products suited to their circumstances.

It’s an approach that brings to mind some of Asia’s biggest digital platforms, including Grab and WeChat, where payments, retail and everyday services sit within the same ecosystem.

There’s no doubt PayPal has been watching the phenomenal growth of these Asian transaction giants.

But PayPal isn’t necessarily trying to become another super-app. Lores sees opportunities in helping Asian small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) sell to consumers in Western markets, where PayPal and Venmo already have established customer relationships.

And with AI agents increasingly expected to shop and make payments on behalf of consumers, trust is becoming a major part of PayPal’s plans.

“I don’t think anybody really owns a customer. At the end, the customer needs to have the ability to choose who they trust,” Lores explained.

He wants PayPal to play a role in verifying AI-led transactions, helping merchants establish that buyers are genuine and protecting consumers when autonomous systems make purchases.

Lores also recognises that new technology and changing consumer habits could pose a bigger threat to PayPal than any single competitor. His answer is to keep experimenting with AI and new payment systems, while being open to partnerships, including with rivals.

“If we need to work with Stripe or Adyen or even other local solutions, of course we are,” he said, “because it’s about presenting our offering to merchants and consumers in a broader way.”

Quite a change from the PayPal checkout button many of us remember.

Asia’s fintechs have their sights set further afield

I end this dispatch with a company that was new to me, but is already a significant player in Asian payments and one that PayPal should probably keep an eye on: LianLian DigiTech.

The Chinese fintech, founded in 2009 and listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange in 2024, helps SMEs process domestic and cross-border payments.

Its chief architect, Jerry Zhou, used SFF to introduce the company’s “From AI Tools to AI Workforce” vision, alongside its new LianLian XWorker platform.

The idea is that AI agents will increasingly operate as a parallel workforce, making decisions, completing tasks and handling payments without needing a person to approve every action.

LianLian wants its cross-border payment infrastructure to support this emerging agentic economy, providing the systems needed to authenticate, authorise and account for transactions carried out by AI.

And LianLian isn’t alone in looking beyond its home market.

One thing I’ve noticed at SFF is just how many Asian fintechs are looking further afield. South Korea’s Hecto Group, Taiwan’s fintech delegation and Chinese companies from Shanghai and Shenzhen are all using the event to signal their international ambitions.

India is also making a big push, with its pavilion designed to help Indian fintechs reach markets across Southeast Asia and beyond.

For LianLian, the growing interest in autonomous AI agents offers another way to bring its payment capabilities to businesses operating internationally.

And what about the humans?

After two days in Singapore, AI is becoming an increasingly prominent part of the conversations about how money will move in the future.

We’ve heard about autonomous agents making payments, tokenised assets trading around the clock and financial institutions preparing for a very different way of serving customers.

Let’s hope there’s still room for humans to play a role in this new world of payments. Not to approve every transaction, of course, but to help set the guardrails, define what trust means and decide what value actually means for us, the consumers.

title: The price of connection: the one question SFF’s payments panel would not answer
snippet: The one question SFF’s payments panel would not answer: who gives up the revenue? The post The price of connection: the one question SFF’s payments panel would not answer appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
A Policy Stage session at the Singapore Fintech Festival promised to say whether the barriers to joining up the world’s payment systems are technical, regulatory or commercial. It spent forty minutes on the first two. The third, who gives up revenue, is the one that decides everything.

The session I had circled on Thursday’s programme was called “The Price of Connection: What It Actually Takes to Build Cross-Border Payment Cooperation”. The title was a promise, and the announcer repeated it as the panel walked on: this was the session that “asks whether the biggest barriers are technical, regulatory, or commercial”.

The line-up could not have been better chosen to answer. Mastercard, Swift, India’s National Payments Corporation (NPCI), Nexus Global Payments and FLAR, the Latin American reserve fund: a card network, a messaging network, a national scheme, a multilateral hub and a regional institution. Between them they sit at every point where a cross-border payment earns somebody money. The moderator, Sourav Ghosal of APIX Platform, promised “really tough” and “provocative” questions.

I came for the third word in that sentence. After two days at this festival I have heard one senior speaker after another say that technology is no longer the problem, and I believe them. I have heard almost as many say the problem is governance. I think that is half the truth. The other half is simpler and less comfortable: every organisation in the chain earns its living from the way things work now, and none of them has yet been asked, in public, what it is prepared to give up.

Named, then dropped

In fairness, the panel did name it. Asked for the hardest part of cross-border payments that is not technology, Andrew McCormack, chief executive of Nexus Global Payments, said commercial incentives, alongside trust, “are probably paramount”. Joyce Bo, Mastercard’s executive vice president for core payments in Asia Pacific, gave the fullest version: “aligning commercial models, economics, pricing, dispute rules, merchant arrangements across markets and competing ecosystems, so that interoperability is commercially sustainable for every participant in the chain”.

That is exactly right. It is also the last time anyone on the stage went near the detail.

Ghosal, to his credit, tried twice. He asked Sohini Rajola of NPCI how the cost of cross-border connection should be shared between schemes, banks, merchants and users. He asked Mike Truter of Swift, about the expensive last mile of a payment, “how do you fix this, and who pays for it?”

Truter’s answer was a description of Swift’s industry playbook and its four groups of actors: policymakers, market infrastructures, financial institutions and technology providers. “Payments is a team sport,” he said. “Everyone has to play.” It is a fair description of the problem. It is not an answer to “who pays”.

Asked what a global card network should do as national QR and instant payment schemes begin to link up directly, Bo began by saying that Mastercard “is not just a card network” and went on to list what it powers and supports: real-time payment infrastructure in the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand, tokenisation, a new agentic payments link in Thailand, the Mastercard Accept launch the day before. All true, and all interesting. But the question underneath was what happens to a card network’s economics when a payment no longer needs the card rails, and that was not addressed.

From there the session moved to the ground every cross-border panel ends up on. Whose fraud rules apply when an Indian traveller pays by UPI in Singapore. How confirmation of payee works across a border. Who carries the loss when an instant payment goes to a fraudster. Settlement finality and FX providers in smaller markets. These are real issues and the answers were competent. McCormack was candid that he did not know of many jurisdictions that had built a working liability-sharing model for instant payments. Carlos Álvarez of FLAR was clear about the gap in fraud standards between countries. But this is the conversation the industry is comfortable having, because nobody’s revenue is at stake in it.

The answer nobody volunteered

The one panellist who came close was the one from a national scheme built to make payments cheap. Rajola refused the cost-sharing question as framed, and then answered a harder one. A cross-border link, she said, has to be faster and cheaper for the consumer and cost the merchant no more, “which basically means that you have to start with everybody else who is in the middle, the intermediaries”, and ask how they make it cheaper. “If there are incentives which don’t align for that, you can have anything on paper as a blueprint. It’s not going to be able to succeed or scale.”

There it was, for about twenty seconds: the money has to come out of the middle. And the middle was sitting on the same sofa. Nobody picked it up.

Nobody on the stage said what their own organisation earns from the friction, or what it would be prepared to give up. Nobody was asked what happens to cross-border card fees when a QR code in Bangkok talks directly to a bank account in Mumbai. Nobody was asked who earns the FX spread and the correspondent fees in Swift’s last mile, and whether those who earn them want that mile shortened. Nobody was asked who sets the price of currency conversion inside a hub like Nexus, or how a scheme stops its members competing the link out of existence. Those were the provocative questions. They are also the ones that explain why the G20’s targets for cheaper, faster cross-border payments are, as the moderator said in his introduction, expected to be missed.

I understand why. Nobody sent to a conference stage by a listed company is going to discuss its pricing in front of its competitors, and forty minutes shared between five speakers is not long. Panellists answer the questions they are given. But the session was sold on the commercial question, and the audience that stayed until late afternoon on day two had earned a straighter attempt at it.

What the evidence says

My own view is blunt. Full interoperability, the kind where a payment takes the cheapest route regardless of whose rail it is, will not arrive by voluntary cooperation between the companies that profit from the alternatives. It is not in their interest, and their shareholders or members would be right to object if they gave it away.

Alan Ni, chief executive of TNG Digital

But it can be done, and the proof was given on this same stage a day earlier, in a session called “Who Builds the Bridge Between National Payment Schemes; and Who Owns the Toll?”. Alan Ni, chief executive of TNG Digital, asked the audience to imagine being one of the biggest payment companies in the country, having spent hundreds of millions signing up small merchants, and believing that network was your moat. Then the regulator arrives. Four or five years ago, he said, Touch ’n Go was the largest acquirer of small merchants in Malaysia, with two million of them, when Bank Negara told the company it had to join the national QR scheme and let every issuer, wallet and bank pay at those merchants, for free.

“It sounds like a very bad thing,” Ni said. “But now, five years later, in hindsight, it might be the best thing ever happened to us.”

His reasons are worth setting out, because they are the commercial answer Thursday’s panel never gave. First, the obligation ran both ways: because Touch ’n Go had to open to everyone, everyone had to open to Touch ’n Go, and its users gained access to every other provider’s merchants. Second, the market grew. QR payments in Malaysia have grown by about 60 per cent a year, he said, and in 2025 overtook both credit and debit cards by value and by number of transactions, and the biggest player took its share of that growth. Third, losing the moat forced the company to compete on something else. With exclusive merchant access gone, it had to become “more innovative” and offer merchants and users better services.

He was not alone in being candid. On the same panel Carrie Suen of Ant International admitted that when Singapore announced its first bilateral payment link, with more planned across the region, “we were worried. What does that mean for our business? Do we still have room to survive?” Over time, she said, the public rails and private networks turned out to be complementary. That is two large incumbents saying out loud what Thursday’s panel would not: that opening up looked like a threat to revenue, and that they are still standing.

Two caveats, in fairness. Malaysia’s example is a domestic one, inside one jurisdiction with one regulator able to give the order, and nobody has that authority across borders. And Ni did not argue that the economics can be ignored. His advice to regulators was to pay as much attention to the commercials as to the rules, because if the price is pushed too low the private sector will not take part. Lawrence Chan of NETS made the same point: the economics have to be sustainable for every party.

So the lesson is not that revenue does not matter. It is that the commercial barrier is real, that the companies concerned will say so when asked directly, and that it was removed in Malaysia by a regulator’s decision, not by a panel of willing partners. The market grew afterwards, and the incumbent is glad it happened.

That is the conversation I wanted on Thursday. If the price of connection is that somebody in the middle earns less, then the honest questions are who, how much, and whether they will do it without being made to.

Asked for one proof point for next year’s festival, Bo said she hoped to see millions of people paying across borders without needing to know which rail sits underneath. Rajola again gave the only number: volumes up 25 per cent and the cost to the consumer down 25 per cent. That is a target you can check.

So here is mine for the organisers. Run this session again in 2027, with the same title and the same companies. Ask each of them one question, and do not move on until it is answered: what did interoperability cost you this year, and did you choose to pay it?

title: LemFi Adds Credit, Savings and eSIMs in Biggest Product Push
snippet: The London remittance firm is expanding into UK credit and savings, backed by its 2025 acquisition of FCA-regulated Pillar, as it targets 304 million The post LemFi Adds Credit, Savings and eSIMs in Biggest Product Push appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
LemFi, the London-headquartered international payments platform, has announced its most extensive product expansion to date, adding a revolving credit line, an instant-access savings account and a travel eSIM service to a platform that already handles around $2 billion in monthly transaction volume across more than 30 countries. The launch is accompanied by a full brand refresh under the tagline “Ambition has no passport” and a rebuilt app.

The company, founded in 2021 by Ridwan Olalere and Rian Cochran, says it now serves more than two million customers, predominantly migrants and diaspora communities moving money across Africa, Asia and Europe. The new products are initially available in the UK, with other markets to follow.

The deal

The credit product is the most structurally significant addition. LemFi is issuing a revolving credit line through Pillar, an FCA-regulated credit provider it acquired in 2025. The facility is available as a virtual card through Apple Pay and Google Pay, and can be used for both spending and international transfers. Eligible customers can also access their Equifax credit score inside the app at no cost, a feature that speaks directly to the persistent problem LemFi is positioning against: credit histories rarely survive a border crossing.

The savings product is an instant-access account opening from £1, currently paying a boosted 5% AER for the first six months before reverting to a 3.04% AER tracker linked to the Bank of England base rate. Deposits are held by ClearBank and protected by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme up to £120,000 per eligible depositor, giving the product a meaningful structural backstop. The eSIM offering, covering more than 100 destinations, allows customers to purchase mobile data before arriving in a new country, removing reliance on local SIM cards or roaming charges.

“Our customers are building careers and businesses in one country while supporting people in another, and the financial system treats them as if they can only exist in one place at a time,” said Ridwan Olalere, co-founder and chief executive. “That is the wrong answer for people this ambitious, so we have rebuilt LemFi to work the way their lives do.”

Market context

LemFi is entering established but underserved territory. The global remittance market, estimated at roughly $905 billion in annual flows, has attracted a wave of specialist platforms in recent years, from Wise and Remitly to newer Africa-focused players such as Sendwave and Nala. Most, however, remain anchored in the transfer product. The move into regulated credit and savings is a less-travelled path and one that raises the compliance overhead considerably. The Pillar acquisition gives LemFi a pre-existing FCA permission set, which shortens the licensing timeline but does not eliminate the capital adequacy and conduct obligations that come with consumer credit.

The approach mirrors a broader strategic pattern visible across several cross-border neobanks: use remittances as the customer acquisition channel, then layer regulated financial products on top to improve unit economics and reduce churn. The question is whether LemFi can execute the compliance requirements of a credit book alongside the operational demands of payments infrastructure across 30-plus corridors. With more than $85 million raised from Highland Europe, Left Lane Capital, Palm Drive Capital, Endeavor Catalyst and Y Combinator, it has the capital runway to attempt it.

The rebrand and app rebuild are clearly designed to signal this strategic shift to investors and potential partners as much as to customers. The next milestones to watch are the rollout of credit and savings beyond the UK, the performance of the Pillar-issued credit book, and whether the eSIM product generates meaningful incremental revenue or operates primarily as a retention and acquisition tool.

title: Why the banks with most to gain from tokenisation move last
snippet: Tokenised money should suit the biggest financial centres best, yet they are the slowest to adopt it. Tim Way of Fireblocks told me why, and what changes it. The post Why the banks with most to gain from tokenisation move last appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
The banks with the most to gain from tokenised money are the ones taking longest to adopt it. London, New York and Tokyo move more money in and out than anywhere else, so on paper they benefit most from putting it on chain. 

Yet most stablecoin volume today flows somewhere else entirely. I put that contradiction to Tim Way, Senior Director for Global Banking at Fireblocks, when we sat down in Singapore this week, and asked whether the hold-up is technology or people.

Friction decides who goes first

Tim Way, Senior Director for Global Banking at Fireblocks

Way’s answer starts with where the pain is. He sees three tiers, central bank money, wholesale markets and retail, each moving at its own speed. Most stablecoin volume today is going to or from the global south or some kind of retail use, he said, “simply because that’s where the most friction today is”.

Wholesale markets have plenty to gain, and he pointed out that the studies showing it have come from banks themselves, not from vendors. But he has also been the person responsible for upgrading a core banking system. “If upgrading a core banking system in one bank is an 18-month effort, then there’s a lot of process, not just technology, that is also required to support digital assets,” he said.

There is a commercial logic to the caution as well. These institutions have very large businesses that they do not want to put at risk. So they are starting in the places where the business case is material, “rather than rewiring the absolute hub of what they’re doing”.

Another ledger, not another bank

I asked whether banks are treating tokenised money as one more thing bolted on to an old core, or as a reason to modernise it. His answer was that it depends on the bank, and that Fireblocks works with both approaches.

Some of the work sits inside the core banking providers. Fireblocks recently announced its work with Fiserv in the United States, where its technology underpins the issuing and holding of stablecoins for Fiserv’s clients. Way expects that to become standard. “The ability to send, hold, receive stablecoins is going to be a necessity for core banking systems,” he said. In the longer run he goes further: “I firmly believe that actually the whole of the core banking stack is eventually going to be reframed.”

Other banks, especially large incumbents, have chosen to run several cores side by side, using providers such as Thought Machine and Episode Six, both Fireblocks partners, to add products quickly on a new subledger. That gave him the simplest description of the technology I have heard. “One way of thinking of digital assets and the blockchain is that it’s another subledger,” he said. “It’s just a subledger for digital assets rather than traditional assets.”

Can one platform handle stablecoins, tokenised deposits, bonds and funds? Technically, yes. Whatever a bank issues, it needs the same security layer and the same control layer: who signs off, what the instruction contains, and whether to release it on chain. The business reality is messier, because the part of a bank that issues debt has little in common with the part that runs receivables for corporates or the part that manages funds. What Way sees at the largest banks is a shared platform that each of those businesses can use. A fungible token built for a stablecoin can be reused for a unit of a fund. A bond that pays coupons on chain needs a different token standard, but it sits on the same foundation.

One set of controls

What banks want from all this is less exotic than the technology suggests. They are not especially worried about the smart contract, Way said. Their question is: “Can I apply the existing control framework that I’ve got across all of my asset classes?” A single control layer means one conversation with the chief information security officer, compliance and operational risk. Without it, “you’d have to have 15 different conversations”.

Regulatory clarity remains the gate. “They’ll do POCs and pilots to prove value, but moving something into production, you’re a bank. You’ve got to be regulatory compliant,” he said.

I suggested that this makes the choice of technology almost secondary. He disagreed. The value stolen in security incidents has risen this year, and “picking the right partner with the right security is paramount”. Banks have firm preferences on how the keys that release a transaction are protected, whether through multi-party computation or a hardware security module, and on whether they run the service in the cloud or in their own environment. Even banks under the same regulator end up with different requirements. “It’s how they choose to comply with the regulations,” he said.

Asia’s opening

The idea I most wanted to test was whether Asia could settle more of its trade in its own currencies using stablecoins. Coming from London, where the eurozone already has its payment networks, I had assumed the banks had long since solved the problem. In Asia they have not.

Way thinks the opportunity is real because tokenised payments change the risk. There is far less time between the intent to pay and the money arriving, so much of the risk that sat in that gap falls away. With every party on one common ledger, the cost of moving between currencies, and between stablecoins and conventional money, should compress. “That’s not what we see today, but that’s an opportunity,” he said.

Europe gains less because one leg of most European trade is already in the eurozone. In Asia both sides are often paying for a currency conversion and routing through New York. “These things are ultimately going to be driven by commercial consequences,” he said. If neither party needs a dollar transaction, that could widen the use of the yen, the Singapore dollar or the Hong Kong dollar to settle trade in the region.

He was careful about the conditions. Regulated institutions at both ends would have to accept the stablecoin, and market makers would need to run deep liquidity between pairs such as the yen and the rupiah, which do not exist today. “I can’t predict where that’s going to go,” he said. “There’s a genuine opportunity here.”

Will customers notice?

My last question was whether any of this reaches ordinary customers. Way’s evidence is in Fireblocks’ own numbers. Two years ago stablecoins were roughly half of the volume on its platform. Today they are 75 per cent. Digital assets, he said, have moved “from being a crypto speculation use case to being a transfer of value use case”.

The benefit is clearest where moving money is hardest, which is why adoption started in emerging markets. It will spread as scale brings costs down. About 1.6 per cent of the US dollar M1 money supply is on chain in stablecoins today, he said. If that reached five per cent, the cost of the infrastructure would be shared across far more participants and the cost of moving on and off chain would fall.

I offered my own comparison, the switch from analogue to digital television: less a revolution than a clunky system quietly replaced by a better one that saves everyone a few per cent. Way added the part I had missed. New rails let new firms into the value chain. Revolut, a Fireblocks customer, changed what people expect from a bank, and he sees no reason for firms like it to stay in retail. “They’re not going to stop at the consumer banking level,” he said.

That is the direction he sees for digital assets as a whole: out of consumer fintech and into wholesale banking.

title: FCA to explore quantum computing to tackle financial crime
snippet: A new initiative will bring together firms, quantum technology providers, and national research labs to explore practical applications of quantum computing. FCA to explore quantum computing to tackle financial crime

              

  

  

  
    

        

    

      

A new initiative will bring together firms, quantum technology providers, and national research labs to explore practical applications of quantum computing.

  

            						

The FCA will bring together financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories to explore how quantum computing could help tackle financial crime.

The Quantum Experimentation Group, the first of its kind for a regulator, will initially explore how quantum machine learning could help detect money laundering and fraud. It will launch in the first quarter of 2027.

Participants will use an FCA synthetic dataset – artificially generated data – to help overcome a key barrier to testing: access to suitable data.

The group will help firms explore practical uses of quantum computing in financial services and share findings to guide future testing. It will also help the FCA understand the technology’s opportunities and limitations, barriers to experimentation and what these could mean for regulation.

Jessica Rusu, chief data, information and intelligence officer at the FCA, said: 'We want to help firms explore where quantum could make a meaningful difference, and early experimentation is essential to understanding its potential in financial services. By bringing together firms, technology providers and researchers we can build readiness and identify practical applications for common industry challenges, starting with financial crime.'

The initiative builds on the FCA’s research into the long-term potential of quantum computing in financial services.

Financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories can register their interest in joining the group by 31 December 2026.

Notes to editors

Read more about the Quantum Experimentation Group and how to register an interest in joining the group.

The FCA’s Quantum Experimentation Group will be the world’s first regulator-led quantum computing experimentation group.

The group will support organisations at different stages of their quantum journey, from those beginning to explore potential use cases to those already undertaking advanced experimentation.

As part of the initiative, the FCA will define problem statements and work alongside participants to build understanding of the opportunities, limitations and practical considerations associated with quantum technologies.

The initiative will complement wider activity across the UK’s quantum ecosystem by creating additional opportunities for collaborative experimentation and learning.

The UK’s National Wealth Fund is reported to be preparing an investment in Uforce, a British defence technology company, just days after the Chancellor allocated an additional £15.4 billion of capital to the NWF in the Budget. The Chancellor simultaneously signalled that the fund should substantially increase its focus on defence, placing the sector at the centre of what the government is calling its “national renewal” programme.

No deal terms, equity stake size or valuation were disclosed in the reports. Uforce’s stage of development and its specific technology area were also not detailed in the available material.

Capital mobilisation and the NWF’s strategic shift

The NWF’s reported pivot toward defence tech represents a meaningful change in the fund’s mandate. The vehicle was established primarily to crowd in private investment for clean energy, housing and industrial transition. Directing it explicitly toward defence-related companies signals that the current administration views strategic industrial capacity and national security as investment categories that justify the same patient, catalytic public capital previously reserved for the green economy.

The move runs alongside a separate reported development: the Chancellor is said to be in discussions about establishing a multilateral financing mechanism with Nato allies, including Finland, the Netherlands and Poland. The proposed structure would raise capital on international markets to fund defence procurement and provide growth finance for domestic defence companies. Ministers are also reportedly considering rules that would require overseas companies winning UK defence contracts worth more than £50 million to invest a matching amount in the UK, a measure designed to strengthen domestic supply chains.

Tom Clarke, a partner in the private equity group at global law firm White and Case, said the NWF move adds momentum for firms seeking to raise funds. “The UK is already home to some of the world’s best defence technology start-ups,” he noted, pointing to White and Case research suggesting that 97% of UK defence and defence technology companies surveyed expect to raise significant external funding within the next twelve months.

The investment landscape for UK defence tech

Private capital has been circling defence technology with renewed urgency across Europe as governments revisit restrictions that previously discouraged institutional and VC investors from the sector. In the UK, a mature venture ecosystem and deep access to global debt markets have positioned the country as a significant destination for this capital, though France, Germany and the Nordic countries are competing actively for the same pipeline of dual-use and pure-play defence technology businesses.

The critical structural question is additionality: whether the NWF’s reported entry into defence tech unlocks private co-investment at scale, or whether it substitutes for private capital that would have deployed anyway given the sector’s current commercial attractiveness. Public development finance is most effective when it de-risks early-stage capital formation in areas where private markets are structurally underweight. Given current investor appetite for defence technology, that case is harder to make here than it was for offshore wind or social housing.

The next markers to watch are the formal announcement of the Uforce investment with disclosed terms, the progress of the proposed Nato multilateral financing mechanism, and whether any legislative instrument follows on the overseas contractor investment requirements. All three threads could materially reshape the capital architecture available to UK defence technology companies over the next twelve to eighteen months.

New resource brings together real-world examples of AI adoption across financial services, helping firms identify emerging trends and opportunities.

  

            						

The FCA has launched a world-first AI Spotlight Observatory that provides firms, academics and innovators with a comprehensive view of how AI is being adopted across financial services.

Based on practical use cases from more than 200 organisations and spanning 150 areas of activity, the online platform highlights how firms are using AI across the industry and where trends are developing.

Developed in partnership with the Centre for Finance, Technology and Entrepreneurship (CFTE) and technology partner NayaOne, the Observatory helps meet the growing demand for greater visibility of AI adoption across the sector.

The resource highlights a range of AI use cases shaping financial services, from solutions designed to combat financial crime and enhance compliance processes to emerging technologies such as agentic payments and neurosymbolic AI.

By widening access to market intelligence, the Observatory will help firms of all sizes learn from developments across the market, better understand emerging technologies and make more informed decisions about adopting AI responsibly. 

Jessica Rusu, chief data, information and intelligence officer at the FCA, said: 'AI is creating significant opportunities across financial services, and we’re committed to helping firms understand how the technology is being used.

'The AI Spotlight Observatory provides an open and accessible resource that brings together real-world examples of AI adoption, helping firms, innovators and researchers learn from developments across the sector and identify new opportunities for innovation and growth.'

Notes to editors

The FCA’s AI Spotlight Observatory is the first resource of its kind for a regulator globally.  

It builds on the FCA’s AI Spotlight Digital Showcase, a repository of practical AI solutions across specific themes, by adding new features and capabilities, such as a common taxonomy for comparison, a distinction between use cases and implementations, and the ability to identify emerging patterns across the market. 

The platform is open and accessible to all users. Registration is required to access more detailed insights, such as target client information, and to request demonstrations directly from innovators featured on the platform. 

The Observatory will continue to evolve through the addition of new use cases. Firms can apply to be showcased on the platform.

CFTE has supported the development of the Observatory across three main areas: creating the taxonomy, building the repository, and socialising the Observatory with the market.  

The Observatory forms part of CFTE’s wider collaboration with the FCA on AI capability, industry engagement and market intelligence. Alongside initiatives such as the Agentic Academy, CFTE supports the FCA in helping the financial-services sector better understand, structure and respond to the opportunities and challenges created by AI. 

NayaOne has been responsible for the design and development of the Observatory platform, including the user interface, navigation, search and filtering capabilities. 

The platform builds on the FCA’s wider work on AI, including its  

AI Discussion Paper, AI Sprint, and AI Lab, which includes AI Live Testing and its groundbreaking Supercharged Sandbox supported by NVIDIA, NayaOne and Anthropic. 

Last month, the FCA published examples of AI good practice and areas of improvement to support the safe and responsible adoption of AI in financial services.

fullText:
Three themes stand out: the growing use of AI, innovation crossing traditional sector boundaries, and financial inclusion.

As firms develop new products, services and business models, many engage with us through our Regulatory Sandbox and Innovation Pathways to understand how regulation applies to their proposition or to test innovative ideas in a controlled environment.

Looking across applications lets us observe emerging trends. It helps us understand how technologies are evolving, and identify emerging regulatory questions.

In turn, this supports our wider work and helps us keep pace with developments across financial services.

Applications at a glance

37% involved AI (up from 31% in 2025), making it the most common technology theme.

92% of the firms engaging with our services were doing so for the first time, highlighting continued demand from new innovators.

64% of proposed solutions included a retail element, showing continued focus on consumer-facing innovation.

The growing use of AI

Firms are focusing increasingly on how to deploy, oversee and govern AI in their business models.

They’re looking at how to use AI to help consumers better understand and manage their finances, support businesses with payment processes, and provide customers with more personalised guidance and support.

Regulation and innovation are working in tandem to deploy new technologies safely and build consumer protection into new products from the outset.

Innovation is becoming more interconnected

Innovation does not always fit neatly into traditional sector categories. While payments and digital assets represented the largest sector-specific portion of recent applications, cross-sector propositions have also been common, representing around one-third of applications.

Many firms are combining technologies, data, payments and consumer-facing services in new ways. As a result, innovative technologies are increasingly crossing traditional sector boundaries and requiring firms to consider how existing governance, accountability, data use and regulatory frameworks apply.

A recent example is our stablecoins cohort in the Regulatory Sandbox. Stablecoin business models often cut across traditional sector boundaries, combining elements of payments, digital assets, and financial market activity. The cohort brought together firms intending to issue UK stablecoins to test how proposed requirements could operate in practice and provide evidence to support policy development.

Financial inclusion

Firms continue to focus on how to improve consumer access to and engagement with financial services. They’re not only exploring new technologies, but also considering how these tools can help address practical consumer challenges.

Applications this year have included propositions aimed at improving consumer understanding, accessibility, personalised support, and access to financial services for underserved groups.

A large proportion of proposed solutions included a retail element, indicating that most firms remain focused on end consumers.

What we’re learning about Sandbox participation over time

We are looking beyond current application trends to understand the longer-term experience of firms that have participated in the Regulatory Sandbox.

Our preliminary research suggests that, as of September 2026, around 71% of them are still active. We are continuing this analysis to better understand the ongoing commercial success of participating firms and whether their original propositions have continued to operate.

We have also been looking to understand at which point of their growth firms engage with the Regulatory Sandbox.

We’ve found that the service is particularly relevant at an early stage of a firm’s development, with around 70% of applications coming from firms that are 0 to 2 years old.

Demand is strongest when firms are still developing their business models, products and approaches to compliance, and seeking to understand how regulation applies as they refine and validate innovative propositions.

Looking ahead

Applications to our Regulatory Sandbox and Innovation Pathways give us an early view of the technologies, business models and the regulatory questions that firms are exploring.

They also provide insight into developments beyond the UK.

We’re continuing to engage with international firms seeking to enter the UK market and sharing insights with overseas regulators and innovation initiatives. This helps us to understand global innovation trends.

The trends we have seen so far suggest that innovation is scaling up, becoming more sophisticated, and more focused on addressing real-world consumer needs.

We’ll continue to engage with firms as technology develops. One way we’re doing this is through thematic cohorts, which explore key areas in greater depth.

Following our Regulatory Sandbox stablecoins cohort, applications to a new climate scenarios cohort opened on 1 October 2026. The cohort invites firms and specialists to test innovative approaches to climate scenario analysis and risk assessment, supporting wider work on sustainable finance and climate-related risks.

Firms developing new ideas should consider how existing regulation applies to their proposition, how they can test and scale innovation successfully, and what safeguards will deliver good outcomes for consumers and markets.

Our innovation services help firms answer these questions. They also let us test policy approaches and gather evidence on how regulation works in practice. This helps inform smarter, more proportionate regulation.

We’re here to support innovators across financial services, helping ensure the UK remains one of the best places in the world to develop, test and scale innovative propositions.

To find out more about our innovation services and keep up to date with future opportunities, visit our Regulatory Sandbox and Innovation Pathways pages.

fullText:
Speech by Sarah Pritchard, deputy chief executive, at TheCityUK National Conference 2026.

  

Speaker: Sarah Pritchard, deputy chief executive

Event: TheCityUK National Conference 2026, Bristol

Delivered: 19 November 2026

Note: This is a drafted speech and may differ from the delivered version.

Reading time: 7 minutes

Highlights

The UK is a global leader in fintech, but we cannot take that position for granted. Firms and regulators alike have to challenge established thinking, embrace uncertainty and try new approaches.

We are changing how we work to keep pace with innovation. That means challenging existing processes, embracing new technology and working with firms to find better ways of doing things.

We encourage firms to come to us early with their ideas. Our Innovation Services are there to help you navigate regulation, test new ideas safely and bring responsible innovation to market.

It’s hard not to feel inspired in a city like Bristol, with its rich history of innovation. 

First, it was aeronautics. Then, it was microchips. Now, it’s fintech. 

Bristol is home to nearly half of all fintech firms in the South West.

Clusters like this one don’t just happen. 

They’re built by people willing to challenge established thinking and take a chance on something new.  

That takes courage.

But for innovation and growth to really thrive, regulators have to be willing to do the same.  

That carries risk. But so does sticking to what we know.  

    

              

How we got here

            						

Our willingness to do things differently in this country has helped make our financial services sector one of the most innovative in the world.

We didn’t get here by accident. 

It took ambitious firms, given the right amount of room to experiment.

The FCA recognised the importance of pushing the boundaries with Project Innovate in 2014.

And the world’s first Regulatory Sandbox in 2016, allowing firms to test innovative ideas with dedicated FCA support.

By 2024, fintech was the most significant job source in UK financial services.

Fintech firms contribute positively to growth, productivity and infrastructure.

No wonder the UK is Europe’s top spot for fintech investment.

But we can’t take that position for granted.

Investment is down. Global competition is up. Funding is getting harder to come by.

And operational disruption is no longer a matter of if, but when.

We’ve recently seen the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange robbed of more than $6 billion.

And a global tech outage that left millions of employees without the tools they need to do their jobs.

Market integrity risks have never been greater.

That's not a reason to hold back on innovation.

If anything, it’s a reason to keep going. We can’t solve these challenges if we stand still. 

But we need to be clear-eyed along the way.

That doesn’t mean certain.

None of us can wait for perfect information.

You decide whether to build, hire or invest before knowing if the idea will work.

We often need to decide whether to act – and how – without the full picture.

Uncertainty comes with the territory.

And in a rapidly changing world, we need to be comfortable making decisions in the face of it.

The decisions that got us here were made that way. The ones ahead will be too. 

          

              

Regulation, growth and innovation  

            						

People often ask how regulation supports growth and innovation.  

But what about regulators?  

Our job is to make sure this sector grows and innovates in ways that create better outcomes for consumers, businesses and the wider economy.  

That means writing rules and working differently: being faster, more accessible, more willing to listen.

And backing experimentation through our Innovation Services, where we help firms navigate regulation and test ideas safely.

We’re seeing results. Firms that enter our Regulatory Sandbox are more likely to raise capital and attract greater investment.

And demand is growing.

We had more applications to the Sandbox and Innovation Pathways in the first half of 2026 than in the whole of 2025 – 92% from firms we haven’t worked with before.

These services are particularly valuable for young firms testing their ideas and business models, with around 70% of applications coming from firms in their first two years.

We’ve scaled and embedded these services across authorisations, policy and supervision. 

Because innovation and regulation are not separate.

          

              

Keeping pace

            						

Markets are changing. So is the speed of innovation.

But so are we. 

Our Innovation Services and the testing they facilitate are faster than sending Q&A between legal and compliance teams, and the regulator.  

And what we learn through experimentation shapes how we regulate and what we share with the market.

You’ve seen this in our approach to artificial intelligence (AI).

Our AI Lab is a place for firms to work with us and explore AI’s potential, risks and opportunities.

It also helps us understand what works.

And today, we’re launching the world-first AI Spotlight Observatory.

Built on cases from over 200 organisations across 150 areas of activity, it shows how firms are really using AI across financial services.  

So you can learn from each other and see where the opportunities lie.

AI could also improve how firms manage risk.

At Mansion House, our chief executive asked whether it’s time to rethink the so-called three lines of defence model: the frontline business, risk and compliance, and internal audit.

I’m taking forward work to explore how innovation could help firms manage risk, grasp opportunities and serve customers better.

That includes better connecting all three lines – with real-time assurance and challenge informed by more timely business insights.

Some firms already use it that way.

Our supervisors are adjusting, too.

As part of being a smarter regulator, we’re modernising how we supervise.

And are looking at whether we ask for duplicative board packs or data that no longer reflects how firms manage risk.

We will also take a step back to understand how firms operate today, and how technology can help us focus on outcomes rather than processes.

Effective risk management is key. 

But it also has to be efficient: timely. Evidenced. Focused on outcomes.

I’ll set out a detailed engagement plan in the coming weeks so we can examine these opportunities together.

Alongside this, our chief operating officer is exploring how to simplify the process around know your customer compliance (KYC).

KYC is an important customer information source, alongside firms’ transaction monitoring, timely investigations of alerts and reporting suspicions.

We know it can feel like the focus is on process over outcomes. 

Now is the time to challenge existing processes and be willing to change what isn’t working. 

If you’re already innovating across your lines of defence or have ideas for simplifying KYC, come and talk to us. 

          

              

Going further 

            						

Our Innovation Services aren’t just for the Next Big Thing. We’re open to any idea that could improve financial services and support growth.

We’re already seeing more firms come forward with ideas.

But we want to hear from firms that haven't used our services much – like those in consumer credit or working on financial inclusion.

That said, not every idea needs our Innovation Services.

Sometimes firms may simply have questions about getting authorised, or the requirements set by various bodies.

That’s why we offer things like our pre-application support service.

And are now letting firms know before authorisation that we’re likely to approve them, helping them secure funding sooner.

We’re committed to working with others to find solutions where a system-wide answer is needed.  

For example, our public statement on safely offering workplace saving schemes, including interactions with our rules and minimum wage requirements.

Our work and our approach reach beyond the UK.

In October, we worked with IOSCO to power its first-ever AI TechSprint, focused on investor education in the age of AI.

Our sandboxes let us test ideas within the existing rules.  

But sometimes the legal framework itself is the barrier. 

Most legislation was written before this kind of technology existed – and it can hold innovation back.

The Digital Securities Sandbox shows what’s possible when rules and legal requirements can be set aside, safely.

It’s a big part of why PISCES, the new private securities market, was up and running so quickly.  

And testing it in the Sandbox means future legislation will be grounded in evidence – not guesswork.

          

              

Take a seat at the table  

            						

There are a lot of conversations happening right now – and there is room for everyone at the table.

So, please, pull up a chair.

We’re making a deliberate effort to get out and hear from stakeholders first-hand.

This year, our executive team alone has made 25 visits across the country.

And we’ve been engaging with consumer groups and firms in Bristol for some time.

Last year, our chief executive met with local fintechs to discuss our strategy and encourage them to use our Innovation Services.

There will be more visits to come.

I know approaching us isn’t always easy.

Too often, firms rule themselves out before they’ve even spoken to us because they don’t have all the answers.

We understand.

But we want to hear from you.

Because while we’re a regulator, we’re also human. And we genuinely want to help.

If you’re innovating, and think your ideas fall within our regulation, come and speak to us.

In return, we’ll listen. Give clear answers. Think differently. And work with others.

Take, for example, agentic AI.

We recently published a joint statement with our partners in the Digital Regulatory Co-operation Forum on protecting people and businesses in an agentic economy.

Because agentic products blur the line between regulated and unregulated activity.

Just because a business describes itself as a technology provider doesn’t mean it can offer financial services without our authorisation.

So, if you're developing or deploying personal agents, come to us early to test your ideas.

We'll move at pace, so responsible innovation can move quickly. 

          

              

Conclusion

            						

The next chapter will be written by those willing to try something new.

Of course, innovation is never without uncertainty. It’s an uncertain world we live in.

Embracing it takes courage – and that’s how we unlock the growth our economy and financial system need.

I doubt those using the Kennet and Avon Canal in the 1800s saw much need for a new way to move people and goods between Bristol and London.

Then came Brunel’s Great Western Railway, which changed everything.

As the most successful entrepreneurs and investors know, sometimes the greatest risk isn’t taking a chance.

It’s standing still.

title: British Business Bank Commits £2m to Cambridge Capital Group via Haatch
snippet: The Regional Angels Programme will co-invest alongside CCG members in every qualifying deal, bringing Haatch's total investment partners to seven. The post British Business Bank Commits £2m to Cambridge Capital Group via Haatch appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
The British Business Bank (BBB) has committed £2 million to Cambridge Capital Group (CCG) through its Regional Angels Programme, channelled via the Haatch Angel Syndicate Platform. The capital will sit alongside CCG’s existing member commitments, co-investing in every qualifying deal the network approves rather than selecting individual opportunities separately.

CCG is one of the longer-established angel networks in Britain. Founded in 2000 and based in Cambridge, it has deployed more than £50 million across over 150 technology-enabled companies during its 25-year history. Members have recorded more than 25 exits from the portfolio. The network is managed by founder Struan McDougall and director Jayne Parker, who oversee both investment activity and portfolio support.

The BBB commitment brings the total number of investment partners on the Haatch platform to seven, continuing what the platform describes as a scalable co-investment mechanism for established angel groups.

The deal mechanics

The structure is worth unpacking. Rather than the BBB writing cheques on a deal-by-deal basis, the co-investment is automatic for qualifying transactions, which means CCG members retain the same sourcing and selection process while the government capital amplifies their collective firepower. This pass-through model is central to how the Regional Angels Programme operates across its partner networks: it tries to preserve the local knowledge and deal-sourcing discipline of the angel group without introducing a separate approval layer that could slow execution.

Mark Barry, senior investment director at the British Business Bank, said the commitment would help “more businesses access the finance they need to scale and grow” by closing gaps in early-stage capital. McDougall described the arrangement as recognition of CCG’s involvement in developing the British angel investment market over its history.

Fred Soneya, co-founder and general partner at Haatch, noted that the platform design deliberately avoids changing how angel groups source and back companies, with the aim of directing more capital to businesses without adding friction for the networks themselves.

Market context

Early-stage equity in the UK regions remains structurally underserved relative to London. The British Business Bank’s own research has consistently identified a funding gap for pre-Series A companies outside the capital, and programmes such as the Regional Angels Programme are one of the government’s primary tools for addressing it without directly picking companies. By working through established networks with embedded local relationships, the BBB bets on the existing deal-flow infrastructure of groups like CCG rather than building a parallel origination capability.

The Haatch platform model sits within a broader trend of syndication infrastructure being built on top of traditional angel networks. Several UK platforms now aggregate smaller check writers and layer institutional or quasi-public co-capital alongside them. The commercial tension in this space is maintaining deal quality and network discipline as capital volumes increase. For CCG, which has maintained selectivity across 150 investments over 25 years, the test will be whether the additional BBB firepower changes the economics of deals it was already doing, or meaningfully expands access to companies that would otherwise have been under-capitalised at the angel stage.

The next metrics to watch are deployment pace under the new arrangement, the number of qualifying deals in the first twelve months, and whether the Haatch platform adds further partners as it pursues the same co-investment model with other regional networks.

fullText:
Global technology event brand GITEX has announced its expansion into South America with the launch of GITEX LATAM, its inaugural Latin American edition. Organised by the Dubai World Trade Centre (DWTC) and KAOUN International in strategic partnership with the São Paulo Development Agency (ADESAMPA) and the City Hall of São Paulo, the event will take place from 16 to 17 March 2027 at Distrito Anhembi in São Paulo, Brazil.

Unveiled during the 45th edition of GITEX GLOBAL in Dubai, the expansion targets a regional digital market projected by PCMI to reach nearly US$950 billion by 2026[cite: 19]. According to International Monetary Fund (IMF) figures, Latin America’s emerging markets and developing economies collectively generate US$6.8 trillion in GDP in 2025, positioning the new summit as an international bridge for cross-border capital, infrastructure investment, and public-private collaboration.

“São Paulo is excited to host GITEX LATAM, a landmark catalyst enabling our finest innovators to meet global opportunities,” stated Ricardo Nunes, Mayor of São Paulo. “This platform will connect pioneering startups, unicorns, and influential enterprises with international markets, unlocking capital, forging partnerships, and expanding visibility on the world stage.”

Brazil’s Digital Infrastructure and São Paulo’s Startup Hub

With Brazil joining an international GITEX network that has expanded across 14 cities and countries in three years, organisers are anchoring the event in Latin America’s largest innovation ecosystem. Brazil has established itself as a prominent adopter of digital public infrastructure, delivering centralised digital services and digital IDs to over 150 million citizens. Looking ahead to 2033, the country’s information and communications technology (ICT) sector is projected to reach US$259 billion (IMARC Group), alongside an artificial intelligence market forecast to hit US$99.8 billion (Grand View Horizon).

São Paulo provides the commercial anchor for the summit:

Ecosystem Ranking: Ranked first both nationally and across Latin America in StartupBlink’s Global Startup Ecosystem Index Report 2025.

Venture Capital Inflows: Attracted more than US$33.5 billion in venture capital funding over the past decade.

Enterprise Scale: Built an entrepreneurial ecosystem valued at US$113 billion that has produced 11 unicorns valued at over US$1 billion, according to Real Instituto Elcano.

“Brazil is the vibrant cornerstone of Latin America’s economy and a distinguished benchmark for dynamic, inclusive, and consequential technology development,” added Trixie LohMirmand, EVP of DWTC and CEO of KAOUN International. “Together with São Paulo – a prolific hub where startup ingenuity, entrepreneurial spirit, and ambitious investments thrive – GITEX LATAM shall integrate Latin America with the limitless digital universe, unlocking unprecedented access to capital, knowledge, tech, and talent.”

“São Paulo awaits GITEX LATAM with tremendous anticipation, not least because of the immense potential to elevate tech cooperation to historic new heights across Brazil and Latin America,” noted Rodrigo Goulart, Municipal Secretary of Economic Development and Labour of São Paulo. “By leveraging the world’s largest network of digital economy relationships – a network universally synonymous with GITEX – we are inspired to cultivate investor confidence and empower entrepreneurs as well as new talents.”

Deepening UAE–Latin America Technology and Trade Ties

The announcement coincides with substantial Latin American participation at GITEX GLOBAL in the UAE, where Brazil serves as the official Country Partner. Trade and investment promotion agency ApexBrasil is exhibiting across two pavilions featuring more than 50 Brazilian startups and innovation hubs, joined by over 10 startups showcased by the City Hall of São Paulo, alongside debut national delegations from Chile and Ecuador.

GITEX LATAM also builds upon strengthened bilateral momentum following the November 2024 G20 Leaders’ Summit in Rio de Janeiro, which marked 50 years of diplomatic relations between the UAE and Brazil and saw both nations pledge deeper cooperation across AI, renewable energy, agriculture, climate change, and emerging technologies. Spanning a programme covering AI, cloud, connectivity, cybersecurity, data centres, agritech, healthtech, and renewable energy, GITEX LATAM aims to connect global enterprises, policymakers, and venture investors with Latin America’s rapidly digitising economies

UK financial watchdogs clarify cyber expectations as attacks rise

              

  

  

  
    

        

    

      

UK’s financial regulators are proposing new guidance to help financial services firms prepare for and recover from cyber incidents as threats grow.

  

            						

The Bank of England’s most recent Systemic Risk Survey cited cyber as one of the risks that would have the greatest impact on the UK financial system. October 2026 saw the second-highest monthly number of cyber incidents reported to the FCA in 5 years, and the highest in the past 18 months, 52% above the previous high recorded in May 2025.

In response, the Bank, FCA and Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) are bringing together existing requirements and lessons from supervisory experience to give firms greater clarity about what is expected of them.

The proposed guidance aligns with recognised cyber frameworks, including the National Cyber Security Centre’s (NCSC) Cyber Assessment Framework. It sets out how firms should manage their cyber risk and resilience without imposing rigid rules, giving firms flexibility in how they meet the expectations in a fast-evolving threat environment.

It covers key areas, including how firms govern, identify, protect against, detect, respond to and recover from cyber risks and incidents. Firms need strong cyber controls to help keep them safe, support well-functioning markets and protect consumers.

Nikhil Rathi, Chief Executive of the FCA, said:  

‘Technology moves fast, and so do cyber threats. The financial sector has a crucial role in tackling those threats, including through products like cyber insurance.

‘Our response shouldn’t always be more rules. Firms have asked us for clarity about what good cyber resilience looks like. This guidance provides it, helping strengthen their resilience, protect clients and the services they rely on.’

Katharine Braddick, CEO of the PRA and Deputy Governor at the Bank of England, said: 

‘Cyber attacks are becoming more frequent, complex and dangerous. Regulators need confidence both that firms have strong cyber controls and that they can detect, contain and recover quickly from incidents. Today’s proposed guidance builds on latest understanding to help firms do that.’

Dr Richard Horne, NCSC Chief Executive Officer, said:

‘We know cyber threats are becoming increasingly frequent and sophisticated, making it more important than ever that organisations can withstand and recover from cyber incidents.

‘The National Cyber Security Centre welcomes this proposed guidance, which will help firms better understand, assess, and strengthen their cyber resilience, in line with our Cyber Assessment Framework.’

Helping firms prepare for AI and quantum risks

Separately, the regulators are publishing additional ‘effective practices’, building on the cyber guidance to help firms practically prepare for specific cyber risks linked to rapid developments in AI and the potential emergence of quantum computing.  

The effective practices include firms tackling vulnerabilities to threat actors using AI, and encourage firms to consider the implications of quantum computing, which could undermine the public-key cryptography that underpins financial transactions.  

These materials reflect the regulators’ position and expertise that allows them to act on the newest risks in the sector, guiding firms through an uncertain and rapidly developing area. 

Notes to editors

The FCA, PRA and the Bank have jointly published a consultation on cyber risk and resilience management.

The consultation closes on 26 February 2027.

Firms, trade associations, technology providers and other interested stakeholders are encouraged to respond. Feedback will inform the final guidance next year.

The proposed guidance is appliable to firms in scope of the regulators' existing operational resilience requirements.  

The approach regulators have taken also reflects the FCA’s focus on smarter, proportionate regulation, providing greater clarity through guidance where new rules are not necessary. This gives firms flexibility in how they meet existing regulatory expectations as cyber risks continue to evolve.

The proposed guidance key foundational cyber risk and resilience areas include:

Embedding cyber risk and resilience in governance and risk management, with clear roles and accountabilities, appropriate board and senior management oversight, defined risk appetite, and regular reporting and assurance.

Identifying and understanding critical IT infrastructure and cyber risk, maintaining up-to-date inventories and maps of critical assets, systems, data and dependencies, and assessing relevant threats, vulnerabilities and potential impacts.

Protecting critical IT infrastructure from cyber threats, applying proportionate controls including secure configuration, vulnerability and patch management, identity and access management, data protection, and controls over third parties and supply chains.

Detecting cyber events and incidents promptly, through effective monitoring and detection capabilities, defined alerting and escalation processes, and regular testing of firms' ability to identify potential attacks.

Responding to and recovering from cyber incidents effectively, with tested response and recovery plans, clear decision-making and communications arrangements, capabilities to contain attacks and restore services, and processes to identify and address lessons learned.

The additional material on AI and quantum computing is not open for formal consultation. However, the regulators are keen to understand from industry whether this type of support is useful and what they would like to see in future.

A recent Bank of England and FCA survey found 88% of respondents expect frontier AI cyber capabilities to have a moderate or high impact on their risk profile over the next 2 years.

In the same survey, 64% said vulnerability management and patching had seen the greatest increase in management attention due to awareness of frontier AI.
